questions.keyConcept: Stylopharyngeus is supplied by CN IX, which passes through jugular foramen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the mucous membrane of:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the mucous membrane of the oropharynx, including the palatine tonsillar fossa and posterior one-third of the tongue. It does NOT supply the nasopharynx (innervated by maxillary nerve via sphenopalatine ganglion), laryngopharynx (innervated by vagus nerve), or larynx (innervated by internal laryngeal and recurrent laryngeal nerves from vagus).
questions.keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal supplies oropharynx, not nasopharynx, laryngopharynx, or larynx.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The following are branches of the vagus nerve in the neck Except:
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve gives several branches in the neck: pharyngeal branch, superior laryngeal nerve, recurrent laryngeal nerve (left and right), and cardiac branches. The carotid body and carotid sinus, however, receive their sensory innervation from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the branch of Hering (carotid branch), NOT from the vagus nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Branches to carotid body are from glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), NOT vagus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding vagus nerve; all are true Except:
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve is the longest cranial nerve, descends within the carotid sheath, has two ganglia (jugular and nodose), and injury causes tachycardia due to loss of parasympathetic tone. However, the vagus is NOT joined by the spinal root of the accessory nerve. Only the cranial root of accessory joins the vagus; the spinal root forms the separate spinal accessory nerve supplying SCM and trapezius.
questions.keyConcept: Vagus is joined by cranial root of accessory, NOT spinal root.
options: It is the longest cranial nerve.
It is joined by the spinal root of the accessory nerve.
It descends within the carotid sheath.
Its injury leads to palpitation and tachycardia (increase in heart rate).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The recurrent laryngeal nerve:
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus nerve (CN X) and descends deep to the pretracheal fascia in the tracheoesophageal groove. It contains motor fibers derived from the cranial part of the accessory nerve (via the vagus) that supply all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid. The right recurrent hooks around the subclavian artery, while the left hooks around the aortic arch.
questions.keyConcept: Recurrent laryngeal nerve contains cranial accessory fibers and supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles.
options: Contains fibers from cranial part of accessory nerve.
Is a branch of superior laryngeal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding the spinal accessory nerve; all are true Except:
questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve arises from the spinal cord (C1-C6/7), enters the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum, and exits via the jugular foramen. It supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. It does NOT contribute to the pharyngeal plexus of nerves; this plexus is formed by glossopharyngeal (CN IX), vagus (CN X), and sympathetic fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal accessory nerve does NOT contribute to the pharyngeal plexus.
options: Arises entirely from the spinal cord.
Enters the skull via the foramen magnum.
Leaves the skull via the jugular foramen.
Contributes to the pharyngeal plexus of nerves.
Its injury in the posterior triangle results in wasting of the trapezius on the same side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Accessory nerve supplies which of the following muscles?
questions.explanation: The accessory nerve (CN XI) is traditionally described as supplying two muscles: sternocleidomastoid (upper part of neck) and trapezius (posterior neck and shoulder). Some sources also describe supply to levator scapulae, but standard dental and gross anatomy teaches that accessory nerve innervates sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding accessory nerve: the following statements are true Except:
questions.explanation: The accessory nerve is a motor nerve. Its cranial part takes origin near the nucleus ambiguus but is distinct from it. Its spinal part runs between the investing and prevertebral layers of cervical fascia in the posterior triangle. The cranial part joins the vagus. However, the accessory nerve (both roots) does NOT emerge at the groove between the pyramid and the olive—that is the exit site of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). The accessory nerve emerges lateral to the olive in the postolivary sulcus.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory nerve emerges lateral to olive (postolivary sulcus), NOT between pyramid and olive.
options: It is a purely motor nerve.
Its cranial part takes origin from the nucleus ambiguus.
It emerges at the groove between pyramid and olive.
Its spinal part runs between investing and prevertebral layers of cervical fascia.
Its cranial part joins the vagus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The hypoglossal nerve:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exits the skull through the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen. It carries C1 spinal nerve fibers that branch off to supply the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid muscles. CN XII does NOT lie within the carotid sheath (it crosses superficially over it), is NOT joined by C2, is purely motor (NOT sensory), and emerges between the pyramid and the olive (not between the olive and ICP).
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve carries C1 fibers and supplies thyrohyoid and geniohyoid; joined by branch from C1 not C2.
options: Emerges from medulla between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Leaves the skull through jugular foramen.
Lies within the upper part of carotid sheath.
Is joined by a branch from C2.
It sensory to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All the following muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve Except:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus (supplied by the vagus nerve). This includes genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus, and all intrinsic tongue muscles. The anterior belly of the digastric, however, is supplied by the mandibular nerve (CN V3) via the nerve to mylohyoid, not by the hypoglossal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior belly of digastric is supplied by mandibular nerve (V3), NOT hypoglossal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The following are cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus Except:
questions.explanation: The cervical plexus (C1-C4) gives four main cutaneous branches: lesser occipital (C2), great auricular (C2-C3), transverse cervical (C2-C3), and supraclavicular (C3-C4). The dorsal scapular nerve, however, arises from the ROOTS of the brachial plexus (C5) and primarily supplies the rhomboids and levator scapulae; it is NOT a branch of the cervical plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal scapular nerve is from brachial plexus (C5), NOT cervical plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The following are branches of the cervical plexus Except:
questions.explanation: The cervical plexus gives branches to the skin (cutaneous branches) and muscles. The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (formed by C5-C6), NOT from the cervical plexus. It supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. All other listed nerves (phrenic, great auricular, supraclavicular, lesser occipital) are cervical plexus branches.
questions.keyConcept: Suprascapular nerve arises from brachial plexus upper trunk (C5-C6), NOT cervical plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The ansa cervicalis:
questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis is a nerve loop composed of fibers from the first three cervical nerves (C1-C3) via descending hypoglossal and descending cervical roots. It lies superficial to the carotid sheath, often crossing the internal jugular vein. It supplies most infrahyoid muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid (but not thyrohyoid, which receives a separate C1 branch via the hypoglossal nerve).
questions.keyConcept: Ansa cervicalis = C1-C3 loop; lies on carotid sheath/IJV; supplies most infrahyoid muscles.
options: Is a nerve loop on the internal jugular vein.
Is formed of fibers from the upper three cervical nerves.
Supplies most of the infrahyoid muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The ansa cervicalis supplies one of the following muscles:
questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis innervates the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid (both bellies). It does NOT supply the thyrohyoid (supplied by nerve to thyrohyoid from C1 via hypoglossal), geniohyoid (C1 via hypoglossal), stylohyoid (facial nerve CN VII), or mylohyoid (mandibular nerve CN V3). Therefore, among the given options, the ansa cervicalis supplies the omohyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Ansa cervicalis supplies sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which one of the following is used as a venous manometer?
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein is a large superficial vein that drains from the posterior auricular and retromandibular veins, crosses the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and empties into the subclavian vein near the clavicle. Because it is superficial, thin-walled, and readily visible under the skin, it is commonly used clinically as a venous manometer to estimate central venous pressure, particularly in patients with heart failure or volume overload.
questions.keyConcept: External jugular vein is used as a clinical venous manometer.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards anterior jugular vein, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The anterior jugular vein begins below the chin from the confluence of the submental veins, descends superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle near the midline, and drains into the external jugular vein jugular arch near the sternal end of the clavicle before emptying into the subclavian vein. The incorrect statement is that it drains INTO the external jugular vein; rather, the jugular arch connects the two anterior jugular veins and then drains into the subclavian vein or external jugular vein.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior jugular vein drains via jugular arch to subclavian vein (not directly into external jugular vein).
options: It descends on the side of median plane of neck.
Right & left veins are united above suprasternal notch.
It drains into external jugular vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards investing layer of deep cervical fascia, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia lies deep to the platysma, splits to enclose the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, forms the roof of the posterior triangle, and surrounds the submandibular and parotid glands. The sphenomandibular ligament, however, is an accessory ligament of the temporomandibular joint derived from Meckel's cartilage ( cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch), NOT from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Sphenomandibular ligament is from Meckel's cartilage, NOT from investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
options: It forms roof of posterior triangle of neck.
It is thickened to form Sphenomandibular ligament.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Superiorly, the investing layer of deep cervical fascia has the following attachments EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia has superior attachments to the superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, mastoid process, and lower border of the mandible. It does NOT attach to the external auditory meatus, which is a cartilaginous and bony canal covered by skin and not by deep cervical fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Investing layer attaches to skull and mandible but NOT to external auditory meatus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia is attached to all the following structures EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia attaches superiorly to the mandible, mastoid process, ligamentum nuchae, and superior nuchal line. Inferiorly, it attaches to the acromion, clavicle, and manubrium. It covers the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles. It is NOT directly attached to the hyoid bone as a specific named attachment point; rather, the pretracheal fascia attaches to the hyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Investing layer does NOT attach to hyoid bone; pretracheal fascia does.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards the prevertebral fascia, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The prevertebral fascia covers the prevertebral muscles (longus colli, longus capitis) and scalene muscles (anterior, medius, posterior). It is attached superiorly to the base of the skull, extends laterally to form the axillary sheath, and lies in front of (anterior to) the prevertebral muscles. The prevertebral fascia does NOT lie in front of the trachea; that is the preTRACHEAL fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Prevertebral fascia covers prevertebral muscles, NOT trachea (that's pretracheal fascia).
options: It is related anteriorly to pharynx.
It is attached superiorly to base of skull.
It lies infront of Scalenus medius.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards the carotid sheath, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The carotid sheath contains the common carotid artery, internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein (laterally), and vagus nerve. It is surrounded by deep cervical lymph nodes and extends from the base of the skull to the mediastinum. The sympathetic trunk, however, lies in the prevertebral fascia POSTERIOR to the sheath, NOT embedded in its posterior wall.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic trunk lies posterior to carotid sheath (in prevertebral fascia), NOT in its wall.
options: It extends superiorly till base of skull.
It blends posteriorly with pretracheal fascia.
It contains internal jugular vein laterally.
Sympathetic trunk is embedded in its posterior wall.
It is surrounded by deep cervical lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards the boundaries of the posterior triangle of neck, choose the INCORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The posterior triangle of the neck is bounded anteriorly by the POSTERIOR border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle (not the anterior border), posteriorly by the anterior border of the trapezius, inferiorly by the clavicle (base), superiorly by the meeting of SCM and trapezius (apex), with a roof formed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia and a floor formed by the prevertebral fascia overlying prevertebral and scalene muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior triangle is bounded anteriorly by POSTERIOR border of sternocleidomastoid, NOT anterior border.
options: Roof - investing layer of deep cervical fascia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All the following are contents of posterior triangle of neck EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The posterior triangle contains the spinal ACCESSORY nerve (not cranial part), trunks of the brachial plexus, transverse cervical artery and vein, suprascapular vessels, external jugular vein, and occipital artery. The cranial part of the accessory nerve joins the vagus nerve within the jugular foramen and exits the skull along with CN X; it does NOT enter or cross the posterior triangle.
questions.keyConcept: Cranial part of accessory nerve joins vagus; spinal part crosses posterior triangle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a tributary of subclavian vein?
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein is a large superficial vein that descends in the neck superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and drains into the subclavian vein proximal to its junction with the internal jugular vein. It serves as a major venous drainage pathway from the scalp and face and is clinically important as an easily accessible vein.
questions.keyConcept: External jugular vein drains into subclavian vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards contents of posterior triangle, choose CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The transverse cervical artery (also known as the cervicodorsal trunk) usually arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery. However, anatomical variations occur where the transverse cervical artery may arise directly from the subclavian artery as a deep branch (dorsal scapular artery). The suprascapular artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk, not the costocervical trunk.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse cervical artery may arise directly from subclavian artery as a variant.
options: Anterior jugular vein ends in subclavian vein.
Subclavian artery lies infront of Scalenus anterior.
Subclavian artery may give deep branch of transverse cervical artery.
Suprascapular artery is a branch of costocervical trunk.
Lymph nodes in lower part of triangle drain posterior 1/3 of scalp.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards submental triangle, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The submental triangle is bounded on each side by the ANTERIOR bellies of the digastric muscles (not posterior bellies), with the base formed by the hyoid bone and the apex at the symphysis menti of the mandible. It contains the submental lymph nodes and the facial artery. Since the boundary should be anterior bellies, stating posterior bellies is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Submental triangle is bounded by anterior bellies of digastric, NOT posterior bellies.
options: Its base is formed by hyoid bone.
It is bounded on each side by posterior belly of digastric.
Its apex is formed by symphysis menti.
It contains the beginning of anterior jugular vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Anterior part of digastric triangle contains all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The anterior part of the digastric (submandibular) triangle contains the submandibular gland, facial artery and vein, hypoglossal nerve, lingual nerve, nerve to mylohyoid, and submandibular lymph nodes. The external carotid artery, however, lies deep to the posterior belly of digastric; while it forms part of the deep boundary, it is not typically considered a content of the anterior digastric triangle.
questions.keyConcept: External carotid artery is not a content of the anterior digastric triangle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards boundaries of carotid triangle, choose the INCORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded superiorly by the posterior belly of the digastric muscle and stylohyoid, posteriorly by the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, and anteroinferiorly by the superior belly of the omohyoid. Its floor is formed by the hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, and pharyngeal constrictor muscles. The roof is formed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Therefore, stating that the roof is the hyoglossus muscle is anatomically incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Roof of carotid triangle = investing fascia; floor = hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, constrictors.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All the following are branches of external carotid artery within the carotid triangle EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Within the carotid triangle, the external carotid artery gives off several branches: superior thyroid, lingual, facial, ascending pharyngeal, and occipital arteries. The posterior auricular artery, however, arises from the external carotid artery near the posterior belly of the digastric muscle, usually above the level of the carotid triangle proper.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior auricular artery arises above carotid triangle, not within it.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match for each muscle in left column with its appropriate nerve supply from right column:
questions.explanation: The infrahyoid muscles and some suprahyoid muscles have characteristic nerve supplies: stylohyoid is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII); thyrohyoid by C1 via the hypoglossal nerve; anterior belly of digastric by the mylohyoid nerve (branch of mandibular nerve V3); sternocleidomastoid by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); and the inferior belly of omohyoid by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3). These nerve-muscle relationships are clinically tested when evaluating cranial nerve palsies.
questions.keyConcept: Specific nerve supplies: stylohyoid = CN VII; thyrohyoid = C1; anterior digastric = V3; SCM = CN XI; omohyoid = ansa cervicalis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match each muscle in left column with its appropriate action from right column:
questions.explanation: The infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles have specific actions: the mylohyoid supports the floor of the mouth and elevates the hyoid; the thyrohyoid depresses the hyoid (or elevates the larynx, depending on which end is fixed); the stylohyoid pulls the hyoid up and back; the digastric elevates the hyoid and depresses the mandible; and the sternothyroid depresses the hyoid bone and elevates the larynx when the hyoid is fixed.
questions.keyConcept: Mylohyoid = floor of mouth support; thyrohyoid = depresses hyoid; stylohyoid = retracts hyoid; digastric = hyoid elevation + mandible depression; sternothyroid = laryngeal elevation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cervical plexus gives muscular branches to all the following muscles EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cervical plexus (C1-C4) gives muscular branches to the scalene muscles, sternocleidomastoid (with accessory nerve contribution), trapezius (with accessory nerve contribution), levator scapulae (dorsal scapular nerve + C3-C4), and infrahyoid muscles via the ansa cervicalis. The mylohyoid, however, is supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3) via the nerve to mylohyoid, not by the cervical plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Mylohyoid is supplied by mandibular nerve (CN V3), NOT cervical plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Superior cervical sympathetic ganglion (SCSG) gives all the following branches EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The superior cervical sympathetic ganglion is the largest cervical sympathetic ganglion, located at the level of C2-C3. It gives communicating branches to the last four cranial nerves (IX, X, XI, XII), pharyngeal branches for the pharyngeal plexus, cardiac branches to the superficial cardiac plexus, superior laryngeal nerve fibers, and external and internal carotid plexuses. It does NOT give direct tracheal branches (these come from the middle and inferior ganglia).
questions.keyConcept: Superior cervical sympathetic ganglion does NOT give tracheal branches.
options: Communicating branches with last 4 cranial nerves.
A cardiac branch to superficial cardiac plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Middle cervical sympathetic ganglion (MCSE) gives all the following branches EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The middle cervical sympathetic ganglion is located at the level of C6, near the inferior thyroid artery. It gives gray rami communicantes to C5-C6, the ansa subclavia (loop around subclavian artery), cardiac branches to the deep cardiac plexus, and branches to the thyroid gland. However, the vertebral artery plexus is formed primarily by sympathetic fibers from all three cervical ganglia, but specifically the vertebral plexus mainly receives input from the middle and inferior ganglia along the artery.
questions.keyConcept: Vertebral artery plexus is primarily contributed by middle and inferior cervical sympathetic ganglia.
options: A cardiac branch to deep cardiac plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion (ICSE) gives all the following branches EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion (often fused with the first thoracic ganglion to form the stellate ganglion) is located at the level of C7 near the neck of the first rib. It gives communicating branches to C7 and C8, vascular plexus around the vertebral artery, cardiac branches to the deep cardiac plexus, and branches to the subclavian artery. It does NOT give pharyngeal branches, which originate from the superior cervical ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Pharyngeal branches come from superior cervical ganglion, NOT inferior cervical ganglion.
options: A cardiac branch to deep cardiac plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards types of fibers within glossopharyngeal nerve, choose the INCORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) carries multiple fiber types: special visceral efferent (styloharyngeus), general visceral efferent/secretomotor (parotid via otic ganglion), general visceral afferent (from carotid body/sinus and tonsil), special visceral afferent (taste from posterior tongue), and general somatic afferent (from posterior tongue and pharynx). It does NOT carry proprioceptive fibers from the salpingopharyngeus muscle; proprioception of pharyngeal muscles is generally carried by the vagus nerve or spinal accessory contributions.
questions.keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal does NOT carry proprioception from salpingopharyngeus muscle.
options: SVA fibers - taste from posterior 1/3 of tongue.
GSA fibers - proprioceptive from salpingopharyngeus muscle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards branches of glossopharyngeal nerve, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve has several branches: the tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve) contributes to the lesser petrosal nerve for parotid secretion; the tonsillar and lingual branches carry sensation from the tonsil and posterior one-third of the tongue (including taste); the pharyngeal branch carries sensory and motor fibers to the pharyngeal plexus; and the muscular branch supplies the stylopharyngeus. However, taste from the anterior TWO-THIRDS of the tongue is carried by the chorda tympani of the facial nerve (CN VII), not the glossopharyngeal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior two-thirds tongue taste is CN VII (chorda tympani), NOT glossopharyngeal.
options: Its tympanic branch shares in providing nerve supply to parotid gland.
Its pharyngeal branch carries sensory fibers.
It gives a muscular branch to stylopharyngeus.
Its tonsillar branch supplies soft palate.
Its lingual branch carries special sensation from anterior 2/3 of tongue

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards types of fibers within vagus nerve, choose the INCORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve contains branchiomotor fibers for pharyngeal, laryngeal, and palatal muscles; general visceral efferent (parasympathetic) fibers that are INHIBITORY to the heart, stimulatory to the gut, and cause bronchoconstriction; general visceral afferent fibers from thoracoabdominal viscera; special visceral afferent fibers for taste from the epiglottis; and general somatic afferent fibers from the external ear. The GVE fibers to the heart are parasympathetic and therefore inhibitory, NOT excitatory.
questions.keyConcept: Vagal parasympathetic fibers are INHIBITORY to the heart (decrease rate/contractility).
options: Branchiomotor fibers - muscles of palate, pharynx & larynx.
GVA fibers - from mucosa of respiratory system.
GSA fibers - sensory from external ear.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: For each vagal branch in left column, choose the appropriate description from right column:
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve has several major branches in the neck and thorax: the external laryngeal nerve (motor to cricothyroid); the recurrent laryngeal nerves (right loops around subclavian artery, left around aortic arch); the auricular branch from the superior vagal ganglion; and the pharyngeal branch from the inferior vagal ganglion contributing to the pharyngeal plexus.
questions.keyConcept: External laryngeal = cricothyroid; recurrent laryngeal encircles great vessels; auricular = superior ganglion; pharyngeal = inferior ganglion.

pairs.target: Begins in neck & ascends in tracheo-esophageal groove.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: As regards accessory nerve, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve has a cranial part arising from the nucleus ambiguus (joining the vagus and exiting via jugular foramen) and a spinal part arising from the anterior horn cells of C1-C5, entering the skull through the foramen magnum, and exiting via the jugular foramen. The spinal part does NOT unite with the cranial part at the foramen ovale; rather, the cranial part exits with the glossopharyngeal and vagus through the jugular foramen, and the spinal part also exits through the jugular foramen but courses independently to supply the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal accessory does NOT unite with cranial part at foramen ovale; both exit via jugular foramen.
options: Its cranial part arises from nucleus ambiguus.
Its spinal part unites with its cranial part at foramen ovale.
It exits from skull with vagus & glossopharyngeal nerves.
Its cranial part is distributed through pharyngeal & recurrent laryngeal nerves.
Its spinal part enters cranial cavity through foramen magnum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The fibers of C1 that join the hypoglossal nerve supply all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: C1 spinal nerve fibers run briefly with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) as a hitchhiker. They supply the meningeal branch to the dura mater of posterior cranial fossa, the nerves to thyrohyoid and geniohyoid, and contribute to the ansa cervicalis as the descending hypoglossi. However, the styloglossus muscle is supplied directly by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) proper, NOT by C1 fibers.
questions.keyConcept: C1 fibers via hypoglossal supply thyrohyoid, geniohyoid, and ansa cervicalis, but NOT styloglossus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe formation of external jugular vein & enumerate its tributaries.
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein is a large superficial vein formed near the angle of the mandible by the union of the posterior division of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein. It descends superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and drains into the subclavian vein near the clavicle. Its tributaries include the posterior external jugular vein, transverse cervical vein, suprascapular vein, and the anterior jugular vein (via a communicating branch).
questions.keyConcept: External jugular vein = posterior auricular + posterior retromandibular; tributaries include posterior external jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, and anterior jugular.
questions.modelAnswer: The external jugular vein is formed near the angle of the mandible by the union of the posterior auricular vein and the posterior division of the retromandibular vein. It descends superficially over the sternocleidomastoid muscle, pierces the deep fascia at the midclavicular point, and drains into the subclavian vein. Its tributaries include: (1) posterior external jugular vein, (2) transverse cervical vein, (3) suprascapular vein, and (4) anterior jugular vein (communicating branch).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate superior & inferior attachments of investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
questions.explanation: The investing layer is the most superficial layer of deep cervical fascia. It splits to enclose the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles and forms a collar around the neck. Superiorly, it attaches to the superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, mastoid process, zygomatic arch, and lower border of the mandible. Inferiorly, it attaches to the ligamentum nuchae, spine of the seventh cervical vertebra, acromion process, clavicle, and the manubrium of the sternum.
questions.keyConcept: Investing layer encloses SCM and trapezius; attaches skull to acromion, clavicle, and manubrium.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior attachments: superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, mastoid process, zygomatic arch, and lower border of the body of mandible. Inferior attachments: ligamentum nuchae, spine of C7, acromion process, clavicle, and manubrium sterni. The fascia splits to enclose the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe attachments & relations of prevertebral fascia.
questions.explanation: The prevertebral fascia covers prevertebral muscles (longus colli and longus capitis) and scalene muscles (anterior, medius, posterior) in front of the vertebral column. It is attached superiorly to the base of the skull near the external occipital protuberance and inferiorly to the mediastinum (T1-T3). Laterally, it extends to form the axillary sheath enclosing the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels. Anteriorly, it is separated from the buccopharyngeal fascia covering the pharynx by the retropharyngeal space. Posterior to the carotid sheath, it covers the cervical sympathetic trunk and the vertebral vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Prevertebral fascia covers prevertebral and scalene muscles; extends laterally as axillary sheath; separated from pharynx by retropharyngeal space.
questions.modelAnswer: The prevertebral fascia covers the prevertebral muscles (longus colli, longus capitis) and scalene muscles. Attachments: superiorly to the base of skull; inferiorly to the thoracic inlet and mediastinum; laterally continues as the axillary sheath around the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels. Relations: anteriorly separated from the pharynx by the retropharyngeal space and alar fascia; posteriorly related to the cervical vertebrae; laterally to the scalene muscles and the emerging trunks of the brachial plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe attachments & relations of pretracheal fascia.
questions.explanation: The pretracheal fascia is a thin layer that lies anterior to the trachea and esophagus. It is attached superiorly to the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage and extends inferiorly to blend with the fibrous pericardium in the mediastinum. It splits to enclose the thyroid gland and invests the trachea, esophagus, and recurrent laryngeal nerve. Its relations include laterally forming the carotid sheath and blending with the buccopharyngeal fascia anteriorly.
questions.keyConcept: Pretracheal fascia encloses trachea, thyroid, and esophagus; extends from hyoid to pericardium.
questions.modelAnswer: The pretracheal fascia is attached superiorly to the hyoid bone, thyroid cartilage, and cricoid cartilage. It extends inferiorly into the mediastinum to blend with the fibrous pericardium. It splits into two laminae to enclose the thyroid gland, trachea, and esophagus, and sends a thin sheet upward to attach to the thyroid cartilage and hyoid bone. Relations: anteriorly blends with the superficial fascia; posteriorly related to the prevertebral fascia; laterally contributes to the carotid sheath.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe contents & relations of carotid sheath.
questions.explanation: The carotid sheath is a condensation of deep cervical fascia surrounding the major vascular structures of the neck. It contains the common carotid artery (medially, below the bifurcation) and internal carotid artery (medially, above), the internal jugular vein (laterally), and the vagus nerve (posteriorly, between the artery and vein). It is surrounded by deep cervical lymph nodes and is crossed anteriorly by the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Posteriorly, it is related to the prevertebral fascia and cervical sympathetic trunk; medially to the trachea, esophagus, and thyroid gland.
questions.keyConcept: Carotid sheath contains carotid arteries, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve; surrounded by deep cervical lymph nodes.
questions.modelAnswer: Contents: common and internal carotid arteries (medial), internal jugular vein (lateral), vagus nerve (posterior, between artery and vein). Relations: anteriorly by sternocleidomastoid; posteriorly by prevertebral fascia and sympathetic trunk; medially by trachea, esophagus, and thyroid gland. The sheath extends from the base of the skull to the thoracic inlet.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe origin, insertion, nerve supply & action of sternocleidomastoid.
questions.explanation: Sternocleidomastoid (SCM) is the most prominent muscle of the neck, forming the boundary between the anterior and posterior triangles. It has two heads: a rounded sternal head from the manubrium sterni and a broad clavicular head from the medial third of the clavicle. Both heads merge and insert into the mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line. It is supplied by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) with proprioceptive fibers from C2-C3. Its actions: unilateral contraction turns the face to the opposite side and tilts the head toward the same side; bilateral contraction extends the head at the atlanto-occipital joint and flexes the cervical spine.
questions.keyConcept: SCM turns face opposite and tilts same side; bilateral = neck flexion + head extension; supplied by CN XI.
questions.modelAnswer: Origin: sternal head from the manubrium sterni; clavicular head from the medial one-third of the clavicle. Insertion: lateral surface of the mastoid process and lateral half of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone. Nerve supply: spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) and proprioceptive fibers from C2-C3. Actions: unilateral contraction turns the face to the opposite side and tilts the head to the same side; bilateral contraction extends the head and flexes the neck.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe boundaries of posterior triangle of neck.
questions.explanation: The posterior triangle of the neck is a clinically important space bounded by the sternocleidomastoid muscle (anteriorly), the trapezius (posteriorly), and the clavicle (inferiorly/base). Its apex is formed by the meeting of the SCM and trapezius. The roof is formed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. The floor is formed by the prevertebral fascia covering the levator scapulae and scalene muscles (scalenus medius and anterior). It contains important neurovascular structures, including the accessory nerve, brachial plexus trunks, and subclavian vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior triangle: SCM + trapezius + clavicle; roof = investing fascia; floor = prevertebral fascia over scalene muscles.
questions.modelAnswer: Apex: meeting of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius superiorly. Base: middle one-third of clavicle. Anterior boundary: posterior border of sternocleidomastoid. Posterior boundary: anterior border of trapezius. Roof: investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Floor: prevertebral fascia overlying levator scapulae, scalenus medius, and scalenus anterior muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate contents of posterior triangle of neck.
questions.explanation: The posterior triangle contains numerous clinically significant structures. The accessory nerve (CN XI) crosses the triangle obliquely. The cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerge at the midpoint of the posterior border of the SCM (Erb's point). The trunks of the brachial plexus emerge between scalenus anterior and medius. The floor contains the levator scapulae and scalene muscles. The triangle also contains the transverse cervical and suprascapular vessels, external jugular vein, occipital artery, and deep cervical lymph nodes.
questions.keyConcept: Contents include CN XI, brachial plexus trunks, subclavian artery, suprascapular/transverse cervical vessels, external jugular, and deep cervical nodes.
questions.modelAnswer: Nerves: accessory nerve (CN XI), cutaneous branches of cervical plexus (great auricular, lesser occipital, supraclavicular, transverse cervical), trunks of brachial plexus. Vessels: external jugular vein, subclavian vein, transverse cervical artery and vein, suprascapular artery and vein, occipital artery, and third part of subclavian artery. Muscles: levator scapulae, scalenus medius, scalenus anterior. Lymph: supraclavicular and occipital lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate boundaries of anterior triangle of neck.
questions.explanation: The anterior triangle of the neck is the triangular space located anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. It is bounded above by the body of the mandible (and the line extending from the angle of the mandible to the mastoid process), posteriorly by the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, and anteriorly by the midline of the neck from the symphysis menti to the suprasternal notch. Its roof consists of the platysma and the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. The floor is formed by the mylohyoid, hyoglossus, geniohyoid, thyrohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid muscles, as well as the constrictors of the pharynx. It is subdivided into four smaller triangles: submental, digastric (submandibular), carotid, and muscular.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior triangle = SCM + mandible + midline; subdivided into submental, digastric, carotid, and muscular.
questions.modelAnswer: Boundaries: anterior border of sternocleidomastoid (posteriorly), midline of neck from chin to sternum (anteriorly), and lower border of mandible (superiorly). Floor: mylohyoid, hyoglossus, geniohyoid, thyrohyoid, sternohyoid, sternothyroid, constrictors of the pharynx. Roof: platysma and investing fascia. Subdivided into submental, digastric (submandibular), carotid, and muscular triangles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate boundaries & contents of submental triangle.
questions.explanation: The submental triangle is located below the chin, between the two anterior bellies of the digastric muscles. Its base is the hyoid bone, and its apex is the symphysis menti. The floor is the mylohyoid muscle. It contains the submental lymph nodes, which drain the chin, lower lip, and floor of the mouth. The facial artery also crosses this triangle, and the anterior jugular vein may begin here.
questions.keyConcept: Submental triangle: between anterior digastric bellies, hyoid base, mylohyoid floor, contains submental nodes.
questions.modelAnswer: Boundaries: between the anterior bellies of the left and right digastric muscles (lateral sides), base formed by the body of the hyoid bone, apex formed by the symphysis menti. Floor: mylohyoid muscle. Contents: submental lymph nodes (drain chin, lower lip, and floor of mouth), facial artery, and origin of the anterior jugular veins.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate boundaries & contents of digastric triangle.
questions.explanation: The digastric (submandibular) triangle is bounded by the anterior and posterior bellies of the digastric muscle and the lower border of the body of the mandible. The floor is formed by the mylohyoid, hyoglossus, and the superior and middle constrictor muscles of the pharynx. Its roof is formed by the investing fascia and platysma. It contains the submandibular salivary gland, facial artery and vein, mylohyoid nerve, lingual nerve, hypoglossal nerve, submandibular ganglion, cervical group of lymph nodes, and the external carotid artery (deep to posterior belly).
questions.keyConcept: Digastric triangle contains submandibular gland, facial artery/vein, lingual nerve, hypoglossal nerve, mylohyoid nerve, and submandibular nodes.
questions.modelAnswer: Boundaries: anterior belly of digastric, posterior belly of digastric, and lower border of mandible. Floor: mylohyoid, hyoglossus, superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors. Roof: investing fascia + platysma. Contents: submandibular gland, facial artery & vein, lingual nerve, hypoglossal nerve, mylohyoid nerve, submandibular ganglion, submandibular lymph nodes, and deep portion of external carotid artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate boundaries & contents of carotid triangle.
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded superiorly by the posterior belly of the digastric and stylohyoid muscles, anteroinferiorly by the superior belly of the omohyoid muscle, and posteriorly by the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The floor is formed by the hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, and the inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles. Its roof is the investing fascia. It contains the bifurcation of the common carotid artery into internal and external carotid arteries; the internal jugular vein; the vagus nerve (CN X); the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); the accessory nerve (CN XI); the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX); the superior laryngeal nerve; the ansa cervicalis; and deep cervical lymph nodes.
questions.keyConcept: Carotid triangle contains carotid bifurcation, IJV, CN IX/X/XI/XII, ansa cervicalis, and superior laryngeal nerve.
questions.modelAnswer: Boundaries: posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid (superiorly), superior belly of omohyoid (anteroinferiorly), and anterior border of sternocleidomastoid (posteriorly). Floor: hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, and inferior constrictor of pharynx. Roof: investing fascia. Contents: common carotid bifurcation, internal & external carotid arteries, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve (CN X), hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), accessory nerve (CN XI), glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), ansa cervicalis, superior laryngeal nerve, and deep cervical lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate branches of cervical plexus.
questions.explanation: The cervical plexus is formed by the ventral rami of C1-C4 spinal nerves. Its cutaneous branches emerge near Erb's point (midpoint of posterior border of SCM) and include: (1) lesser occipital (C2), (2) great auricular (C2-C3), (3) transverse cervical (C2-C3), and (4) supraclavicular (C3-C4). Its muscular branches include the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3), phrenic nerve (C3-C5), segmental branches to prevertebral and scalene muscles, branches to sternocleidomastoid (with CN XI contribution), trapezius (with CN XI contribution), levator scapulae, and the nerve to rhomboids (dorsal scapular nerve, C4-C5).
questions.keyConcept: Cervical plexus branches: 4 cutaneous (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, supraclavicular) and muscular (ansa cervicalis, phrenic, dorsal scapular).
questions.modelAnswer: Cutaneous branches: (1) lesser occipital (C2), (2) great auricular (C2-C3), (3) transverse cervical (C2-C3), (4) supraclavicular (C3-C4). Muscular branches: ansa cervicalis (C1-C3), phrenic nerve (C3-C5), branches to sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (with CN XI), levator scapulae, dorsal scapular nerve to rhomboids (C4-C5), and segmental branches to scalene muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Give a short account on ansa cervicalis.
questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis is a nerve loop in the anterior triangle of the neck formed by the descending hypoglossal nerve (C1 fibers traveling with the hypoglossal nerve) and the descending cervical nerve (C2-C3 fibers from the cervical plexus). It lies superficial to the internal jugular vein and carotid sheath. It innervates the infrahyoid muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid (both bellies). The thyrohyoid and geniohyoid are supplied by separate branches from C1.
questions.keyConcept: Ansa cervicalis = C1 + C2-C3 loop on carotid sheath; supplies sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid.
questions.modelAnswer: The ansa cervicalis is formed by the union of a descending branch from the cervical plexus (C2-C3) and a descending branch of the hypoglossal nerve (descending hypoglossi) containing C1 fibers. It lies on the anterior wall of the carotid sheath. It supplies the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid muscles (both bellies of omohyoid). The thyrohyoid and geniohyoid receive direct C1 branches via the hypoglossal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate branches of superior cervical sympathetic ganglion (SCSG).
questions.explanation: The superior cervical sympathetic ganglion (SCSG) is the largest cervical ganglion, located at the level of C1-C3 and the internal carotid artery. Its branches include: (1) gray rami communicantes to C1-C4 spinal nerves; (2) a branch to the internal carotid artery forming the internal carotid plexus (distributed to the eye and blood vessels of the head); (3) branches to the external carotid artery; (4) the pharyngeal branch contributing to the pharyngeal plexus; (5) superior laryngeal nerve; (6) cardiac branches to the superficial cardiac plexus; and (7) communicating branches to the last four cranial nerves (IX, X, XI, XII).
questions.keyConcept: SCSG branches: gray rami C1-C4, internal/external carotid plexuses, pharyngeal branch, superior laryngeal, cardiac.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of SCSG: (1) gray rami to C1-C4; (2) internal carotid plexus to eye and head vessels; (3) external carotid plexus; (4) pharyngeal plexus branch; (5) superior laryngeal nerve; (6) cardiac branches to superficial cardiac plexus; (7) communicating branches to last four cranial nerves (glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, hypoglossal).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate branches of middle cervical sympathetic ganglion (MCSG).
questions.explanation: The middle cervical sympathetic ganglion (MCSG) is a small ganglion located at the level of the sixth cervical vertebra, usually near the inferior thyroid artery. Its branches include: (1) gray rami communicantes to the fifth and sixth cervical spinal nerves; (2) the ansa subclavia, a nerve loop around the subclavian artery; (3) thyroid branches accompanying the inferior thyroid artery; (4) a cardiac branch to the deep cardiac plexus; and (5) esophageal and tracheal branches.
questions.keyConcept: MCSG branches: gray rami C5-C6, ansa subclavia, thyroid branches, cardiac to deep plexus, and esophageal/bronchial branches.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of MCSG: (1) gray rami to C5 and C6; (2) ansa subclavia (loop around subclavian artery); (3) thyroid branches (with inferior thyroid artery); (4) cardiac branch to deep cardiac plexus; (5) esophageal and tracheal branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate branches of inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion (ICSG).
questions.explanation: The inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion (ICSG) is usually fused with the first thoracic ganglion to form the cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglion at the neck of the first rib. Its branches include: (1) gray rami communicantes to C7-C8 and T1; (2) a vascular plexus around the vertebral artery (vertebral plexus); (3) plexuses around the subclavian and axillary arteries; (4) cardiac branches to the deep cardiac plexus; and (5) tracheal, esophageal, and bronchial branches.
questions.keyConcept: ICSG branches: gray rami C7-C8-T1, vertebral plexus, subclavian plexus, cardiac branches, and tracheal/bronchial branches.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of ICSG (often fused with T1 to form stellate ganglion): (1) gray rami to C7, C8, and T1; (2) vertebral artery plexus; (3) subclavian and axillary artery plexuses; (4) cardiac branches to deep cardiac plexus; (5) tracheal, esophageal, and bronchial branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate branches of glossopharyngeal nerve.
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) has several branches: (1) tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve) to the middle ear, forming the tympanic plexus; (2) lesser petrosal nerve (from tympanic plexus) to the otic ganglion for parotid gland secretion; (3) carotid branch (nerve of Hering) to the carotid body and carotid sinus; (4) pharyngeal branches contributing to the pharyngeal plexus; (5) tonsillar branches to the palatine tonsils; (6) lingual branches to the posterior one-third of the tongue (general sensation and taste); and (7) muscular branch to the stylopharyngeus muscle.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX branches: tympanic, lesser petrosal, carotid, pharyngeal, tonsillar, lingual, and stylopharyngeus.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of glossopharyngeal nerve: (1) tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve); (2) lesser petrosal nerve (to otic ganglion); (3) carotid branch (nerve of Hering); (4) pharyngeal branches; (5) tonsillar branches; (6) lingual branches (posterior 1/3 tongue); (7) muscular branch to stylopharyngeus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate branches of superior & inferior vagal ganglia.
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve has a superior (jugular) ganglion and an inferior (nodose) ganglion in the neck. The superior vagal ganglion gives off the auricular branch (Arnold's nerve), which supplies sensation to the skin of the external acoustic meatus and the tympanic membrane, and the meningeal branch to the posterior cranial fossa dura. The inferior vagal ganglion gives rise to: the pharyngeal branch (joins pharyngeal plexus), the superior laryngeal nerve (dividing into external and internal branches), cardiac branches (to superficial and deep cardiac plexuses), and the recurrent laryngeal nerve (right loops around subclavian, left loops around aorta).
questions.keyConcept: Superior ganglion: auricular and meningeal branches. Inferior ganglion: pharyngeal, superior laryngeal, cardiac, recurrent laryngeal, and visceral branches.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior vagal ganglion branches: (1) auricular branch (Arnold's nerve), (2) meningeal branch. Inferior vagal ganglion branches: (1) pharyngeal branch, (2) superior laryngeal nerve (external and internal), (3) cardiac branches, (4) recurrent laryngeal nerve, (5) bronchial, esophageal, and gastric branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate branches of vagus nerve in neck & thorax.
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve gives multiple branches as it descends through the neck and thorax. In the neck: meningeal branch, auricular branch (Arnold's nerve), pharyngeal branches, superior laryngeal nerve (external and internal), recurrent laryngeal nerve (left hooks around aortic arch, right hooks around subclavian artery), and cardiac branches. In the thorax: recurrent laryngeal nerves (also in thorax), cardiac branches, pulmonary branches, and esophageal plexus branches. In the abdomen: gastric branches (anterior and posterior), hepatic branches, celiac branches, renal branches, and intestinal branches.
questions.keyConcept: Vagus branches: neck (auricular, pharyngeal, superior laryngeal, recurrent laryngeal, cardiac), thorax (cardiac, pulmonary, esophageal), abdomen (gastric, hepatic, celiac).
questions.modelAnswer: Neck branches: meningeal, auricular (Arnold's nerve), pharyngeal, superior laryngeal nerve, recurrent laryngeal nerve (left around aorta, right around subclavian), cardiac branches. Thoracic branches: cardiac, pulmonary, esophageal plexus, recurrent laryngeal. Abdominal branches: anterior and posterior gastric, hepatic, celiac, renal, and intestinal branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe cranial & spinal parts of accessory nerve.
questions.explanation: The accessory nerve (CN XI) has two distinct parts. The cranial part arises from the nucleus ambiguus in the medulla oblongata, exits via the jugular foramen, and joins the vagus nerve. Its fibers are distributed with the vagus via the pharyngeal and recurrent laryngeal branches to supply the muscles of the palate, pharynx, and larynx. The spinal part arises from the spinal accessory nucleus in the lateral horn of the upper five or six cervical spinal cord segments, ascends through the foramen magnum, exits via the jugular foramen, descends in the posterior triangle, and supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Cranial accessory = nucleus ambiguus → vagus → pharyngeal + recurrent laryngeal. Spinal accessory = C1-C5 → SCM + trapezius.
questions.modelAnswer: Cranial part: arises from nucleus ambiguus in medulla, exits via jugular foramen, joins vagus nerve, and is distributed via pharyngeal and recurrent laryngeal branches to supply muscles of palate, pharynx, and larynx. Spinal part: arises from spinal accessory nucleus (C1-C5/6), enters cranial cavity through foramen magnum, exits via jugular foramen, descends posteriorly in neck through posterior triangle, and supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate branches of hypoglossal nerve.
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) emerges from the hypoglossal canal above the occipital condyle, descends between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein, and curves forward above the hyoid bone to reach the tongue. Its branches include: (1) meningeal branch to the dura of posterior cranial fossa; (2) descending hypoglossi (C1 fibers) contributing to the ansa cervicalis; (3) nerve to thyrohyoid (C1 fibers); (4) nerve to geniohyoid (C1 fibers); and (5) lingual branches to the muscles of the tongue (hyoglossus, genioglossus, styloglossus, and intrinsic tongue muscles).
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal branches: meningeal, C1 to ansa cervicalis, C1 to thyrohyoid/geniohyoid, lingual branches to tongue muscles.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of hypoglossal nerve: (1) meningeal branch to posterior cranial fossa dura; (2) descending hypoglossi (C1 fibers to ansa cervicalis); (3) nerve to thyrohyoid (C1); (4) nerve to geniohyoid (C1); (5) lingual branches to all extrinsic and intrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus (genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus, superior/inferior longitudinal, transverse, vertical).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the boundaries & the floor of the carotid triangle of the neck.
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle is one of the subdivisions of the anterior triangle of the neck. Its boundaries are formed by important muscles that define the surgical approach to the carotid vessels and cranial nerves. The floor muscles include the hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, and the inferior constrictor of the pharynx, which are clinically relevant during surgical dissection in this area.
questions.keyConcept: Carotid triangle floor: hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, sternohyoid, inferior pharyngeal constrictor, and thyroid.
questions.modelAnswer: Boundaries: superiorly by posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid; anteroinferiorly by superior belly of omohyoid; posteriorly by anterior border of sternocleidomastoid. Floor: hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, sternohyoid (superior part), inferior constrictor of pharynx, and thyroid gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: List the vessels present in the posterior triangle of the neck
questions.explanation: The posterior triangle of the neck is a significant anatomical area containing several important vessels. Venous structures include the external jugular vein, subclavian vein, and various tributaries such as the transverse cervical, suprascapular, and anterior jugular veins. Arterial structures include the third part of the subclavian artery, occipital artery, and the transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior triangle vessels: EJV, subclavian, transverse cervical, suprascapular, occipital, and third part of subclavian artery.
questions.modelAnswer: Veins: external jugular vein, subclavian vein, internal jugular vein (deep), transverse cervical vein, suprascapular vein, anterior jugular vein, and posterior external jugular vein. Arteries: third part of subclavian artery, occipital artery, transverse cervical artery, suprascapular artery, and superficial cervical artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate muscles attached to styloid process & nerve supply of each.
questions.explanation: Three muscles are attached to the styloid process of the temporal bone. These muscles are important in swallowing and tongue movement. The stylohyoid elevates and retracts the hyoid bone during swallowing. The styloglossus retracts and elevates the tongue. The stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx during swallowing and speech. Their nerve supplies reflect their embryological origins from different pharyngeal arches.
questions.keyConcept: Styloid process muscles: stylohyoid (CN VII, arch II), styloglossus (CN XII, arch I), stylopharyngeus (CN IX, arch III).
questions.modelAnswer:
Muscles attached to styloid process:
A) Stylohyoid = facial nerve.
B) Styloglossus = hypoglossal nerve.
C) Stylopharyngeus = pharyngeal branch of vagus (cranial accessory).

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: A patient when asked to protrude his tongue outside the mouth cavity the doctor observed that the tip of tongue is directed to the left side. Facial muscles & rest of body muscles were normal.
questions.explanation: Tongue deviation to one side upon protrusion is a classic clinical sign of an ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) lower motor neuron lesion. The genioglossus muscle on the affected side is paralyzed and cannot push the tongue forward, so the healthy contralateral genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the weak side. The facial muscles and body being normal rules out a facial nerve (CN VII) lesion or generalized weakness.
questions.keyConcept: Tongue deviation toward lesion side = ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve palsy; exits via hypoglossal canal.

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] Name the injured nerve.
[TYPE: essay] Mention the side of the lesion.
[TYPE: essay] Mention how this nerve exits the skull.

questions.modelAnswer:
SubQuestions:
1. Left hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
2. Left side (the tip deviates toward the side of the lesion).
3. It exits the skull through the hypoglossal canal (canal for the hypoglossal nerve, located above the occipital condyle and anterosuperolateral to the foramen magnum).

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: A passenger sitting beside an open window suddenly developed spasmodic pain in his neck accompanied by turning of his face to the right side.
questions.explanation: Spasmodic torticollis (wry neck) is characterized by painful, spasmodic contraction of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, causing the face to turn to the contralateral side or the same side depending on which head contracts. When the face turns to the right side, the LEFT sternocleidomastoid is contracting (rotating the face to the right). However, some texts describe the condition with the face turning toward the contracting muscle's side. The classic description of torticollis involves sternocleidomastoid spasm.
questions.keyConcept: Torticollis = sternocleidomastoid spasm; supplied by spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); enclosed by investing layer.

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] Name the affected muscle and its side.
[TYPE: essay] Mention its nerve supply.
[TYPE: essay] Name the fascia enclosing this muscle.

questions.modelAnswer:
SubQuestions:
1. Sternocleidomastoid muscle, right side (the face turning to the right indicates contraction of the right sternocleidomastoid).
2. Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).
3. Investing layer of deep cervical fascia.

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: A 50 year old male started to complain from difficulty in swallowing few weeks ago. He had a computerized tomography scan (CT scan) on the neck done; it revealed the presence of a swelling (most likely cancer) near the jugular foramen.
questions.explanation: A jugular foramen tumor (glomus jugulare or skull base metastasis) can compress the glossopharyngeal (CN IX), vagus (CN X), and accessory (CN XI) nerves (Vernet's syndrome). Dysphagia results from involvement of the pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves that form the pharyngeal plexus and are essential for pharyngeal contraction during swallowing. Additionally, the inferior petrosal sinus (which drains from cavernous sinus) and the sigmoid sinus drain through the jugular foramen into the internal jugular vein and are endangered by tumor growth.
questions.keyConcept: Jugular foramen lesion (Vernet's syndrome) affects CN IX/X/XI; endangers inferior petrosal and sigmoid sinuses.

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] In this patient, which nerves could be involved & led to dysphagia?
[TYPE: essay] Which venous sinuses are endangered by the cancer?

questions.modelAnswer:
SubQuestions:
1. Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and vagus nerve (CN X). Loss of pharyngeal plexus function due to lesion at jugular foramen (Vernet's syndrome).
2. Inferior petrosal sinus and sigmoid sinus (both drain through the jugular foramen into the internal jugular vein).

questions.subject: Clinical
questions.text: A 54 years old man presented with a tumor in the posterior cranial fossa. The neurologist wanted to check the integrity of the 9th, 10th and 11th cranial nerves.
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) is tested clinically by asking the patient to say 'ah' while observing palatal elevation (uvula should remain midline or deviate to the unaffected side), checking the gag reflex (afferent limb via CN IX, efferent via CN X), and checking the cough reflex. The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste from the posterior one-third of the tongue and general sensation from the tonsillar fossa; its sensory branches include the tympanic, tonsillar, lingual, and carotid branches. The accessory nerve supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Vagus tested by palatal movement/gag reflex; glossopharyngeal sensory = tympanic, carotid, tonsillar, lingual; accessory = SCM + trapezius.

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] How can you test for integrity of vagus nerve?
[TYPE: essay] Enumerate sensory branches of glossopharyngeal nerve.
[TYPE: essay] Name the muscle(s) supplied by accessory nerve.

questions.modelAnswer:
SubQuestions:
1. Ask patient to say 'ah' and observe palatal elevation (asymmetry indicates vagus palsy); test gag reflex (afferent CN IX, efferent CN X); observe for hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal involvement).
2. Sensory branches: tympanic branch (to middle ear), carotid branch (to carotid body/sinus), pharyngeal branch, tonsillar branch, and lingual branch (posterior 1/3 tongue taste and sensation).
3. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Blockage of CSF flow between the 3rd & 4th ventricles involves the:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius is a narrow channel穿过 midbrain connecting the 3rd and 4th ventricles. Blockage of CSF flow between these ventricles occurs at the aqueduct, causing aqueductal stenosis and non-communicating hydrocephalus. The interventricular foramen connects lateral to 3rd ventricle; foramina of Magendie and Luschka connect 4th ventricle to subarachnoid space.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius connects 3rd and 4th ventricles; blockage causes non-communicating hydrocephalus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nuclei relays auditory impulses?
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate body is a thalamic relay nucleus for auditory information. It receives input from the inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projects via acoustic radiation to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. The lateral geniculate body relays visual impulses, not auditory.
questions.keyConcept: Medial geniculate body relays auditory impulses from inferior colliculus to auditory cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The fourth ventricle is connected to the third ventricle by:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius is the narrow channel that passes through the midbrain and connects the third ventricle anteriorly with the fourth ventricle posteriorly. It is flanked by the cerebral peduncles and is the most common site of obstruction in non-communicating hydrocephalus.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct connects 3rd ventricle (anterior) with 4th ventricle (posterior).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following thalamic nuclei has a motor function?
questions.explanation: The ventral lateral (VL) thalamic nucleus is the primary motor relay nucleus. It receives input from the cerebellum (via dentatothalamic tract) and basal ganglia (via medial globus pallidus internus) and projects to the motor cortex. It helps coordinate voluntary movement planning and execution.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral lateral (VL) nucleus is the motor relay nucleus of the thalamus; receives cerebellar and basal ganglia input.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Thalamic nucleus that relays cerebellar output:
questions.explanation: The ventral lateral thalamic nucleus receives input from the deep cerebellar nuclei (dentate, emboliform, globose nuclei) via the superior cerebellar peduncle and dentatothalamic tract. It then projects to the motor and premotor cortices, serving as the cerebellar relay to the cerebrum.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral lateral nucleus relays cerebellar output to the cerebral cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following shares in forming lateral wall of third ventricle?
questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the third ventricle is formed superiorly by the thalamus and inferiorly by the hypothalamus, separated by the hypothalamic sulcus. The hypothalamus forms the floor and contributes to the anterior wall. The epithalamus forms the posterior wall. Lamina terminalis forms the anterior wall.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral wall of 3rd ventricle is formed by thalamus (superior) and hypothalamus (inferior), separated by hypothalamic sulcus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following thalamic nuclei is related to the limbic system?
questions.explanation: The anterior thalamic nucleus is a key component of the limbic system Papez circuit, which includes the hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, and cingulate gyrus. It receives input from the hippocampus via the fornix and mammillothalamic tract, and projects to the cingulate gyrus, playing a central role in emotion and memory.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior thalamic nucleus is part of Papez circuit (limbic system); connected to hippocampus and cingulate gyrus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The thalamic nucleus that relays pain and temperature sensations from the head is the:
questions.explanation: The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus receives somatosensory input specifically from the head and face. It receives the trigeminal lemniscus (carrying pain, temperature, and touch from the face) and projects to the primary somatosensory cortex. VPL handles the body; VPM handles the face.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus relays pain, temperature, and touch sensations specifically from the HEAD and face.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The anterior thalamic nucleus is connected to the:
questions.explanation: The anterior thalamic nucleus receives major input from the mammillary bodies via the mammillothalamic tract. The mammillary bodies receive input from the hippocampus via the fornix, completing the Papez circuit of the limbic system. It also projects back to the hippocampus indirectly.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior thalamic nucleus is connected to hypothalamus via mammillothalamic tract and Papez circuit.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is (are) included in the metathalamus:
questions.explanation: The metathalamus is the posterior part of the thalamus consisting of the medial and lateral geniculate bodies. The medial geniculate body relays auditory information; the lateral geniculate body relays visual information. The epithalamus (pineal body, habenular nuclei, posterior commissure) is a separate division.
questions.keyConcept: Metathalamus consists of medial and lateral geniculate bodies; relays auditory and visual impulses respectively.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The medial surface of thalamus:
questions.explanation: The medial surface of the thalamus forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle, is limited inferiorly by the hypothalamic sulcus, and the two thalami are connected in about 80% of individuals by an interthalamic adhesion (massa intermedia). All the listed statements about the medial surface are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Medial surface of thalamus: forms lateral wall of 3rd ventricle, bounded below by hypothalamic sulcus, connected to opposite thalamus by interthalamic adhesion.
options: Is limited inferiorly by hypothalamic sulcus.
Is connected to the opposite surface by interthalamic adhesions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Epithalamus is formed of:
questions.explanation: The epithalamus is the posterior portion of the thalamus comprising the pineal body, habenular nuclei, habenular commissure, and posterior commissure. It is involved in circadian rhythm regulation (via pineal melatonin secretion) and emotional processing related to the limbic system.
questions.keyConcept: Epithalamus comprises pineal body, habenular nuclei, and posterior commissure; regulates circadian rhythms.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The lateral wall of the third ventricle is formed by:
questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the third ventricle is formed superiorly by the thalamus and inferiorly by the hypothalamus, separated by the hypothalamic sulcus. Neither the lamina terminalis nor the anterior commissure forms the lateral wall; they are part of the anterior wall and intraventricular structures respectively.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral wall of 3rd ventricle is formed by thalamus (superior part) and hypothalamus (inferior part).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nucleus ventralis posterior of thalamus receives the following Except:
questions.explanation: Nucleus ventralis posterior (VP) of the thalamus receives medial lemniscus (body tactile/proprioceptive), spinal lemniscus (body pain/temperature), trigeminal lemniscus (face sensation), and fibers from nucleus solitarius (gustatory). The lateral lemniscus carries auditory information to the inferior colliculus, NOT to VP nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: VP nucleus receives medial lemniscus, spinal lemniscus, trigeminal lemniscus, and gustatory fibers; lateral lemniscus goes to inferior colliculus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nucleus ventralis posterior medialis (VPM) of thalamus receives:
questions.explanation: The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus receives the trigeminal lemniscus carrying pain, temperature, and touch sensation from the face and head. It also receives gustatory fibers from the nucleus solitarius. The medial lemniscus and spinal lemniscus terminate in VPL, not VPM.
questions.keyConcept: VPM receives trigeminal lemniscus (face sensation) and gustatory fibers from nucleus solitarius.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The thalamic nucleus for pain and temperature sensations of head is:
questions.explanation: The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus is the specific relay center for pain, temperature, and crude touch sensations from the head (face, scalp, meninges, and oral cavity). It receives input from the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve via the trigeminal lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: VPM nucleus relays pain and temperature sensations specifically from the HEAD via trigeminal lemniscus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The thalamic nucleus in which spinal & medial lemnisci terminate is:
questions.explanation: The ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus is the thalamic relay for somatosensory information from the body. Both the medial lemniscus (carrying fine touch and proprioception from the body) and the spinal lemniscus (carrying pain and temperature from the body) terminate in the VPL nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: VPL nucleus is where spinal lemniscus (pain/temp from body) and medial lemniscus (touch/proprioception from body) terminate.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Sensations received by the thalamus include all the following Except:
questions.explanation: The thalamus acts as a relay station for almost all sensory modalities (except olfaction) on their way to the cerebral cortex. It receives exteroceptive, proprioceptive, gustatory, visual, and auditory sensations. Olfaction (smell) is the only sensory modality that does not relay through the thalamus—olfactory signals go directly to the olfactory bulb and limbic system.
questions.keyConcept: All major sensations relay through thalamus EXCEPT smell; olfactory pathway bypasses thalamus to limbic system.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the following structures does not contribute to floor of 3rd Ventricle:
questions.explanation: The floor of the third ventricle (from anterior to posterior) is formed by the optic chiasma, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, and posterior perforated substance. The lamina terminalis forms the AN anterior wall of the third ventricle, not the floor. The optic chiasma lies just above the pituitary stalk at the anterior aspect of the ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Lamina terminalis forms anterior wall of 3rd ventricle, NOT the floor. Floor = optic chiasma, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following surfaces (aspects) of thalamus is related to posterior limb of internal capsule?
questions.explanation: The lateral surface of the thalamus is related to the posterior limb of the internal capsule. The internal capsule carries corticospinal, corticopontine, thalamocortical, and corticothalamic fibers between the thalamus and the cerebral cortex. The superior thalamic surface relates to the body of lateral ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral surface of thalamus is related to posterior limb of internal capsule (contains thalamocortical and corticospinal fibers).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following thalamic nuclei relays motor impulses?
questions.explanation: The ventral anterior (VA) nucleus is a motor-related thalamic nucleus that receives input from the basal ganglia (via the medial globus pallidus internus) and projects to the premotor and motor cortices. It plays a role in motor planning and initiation. VA and VL together form the motor thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral anterior (VA) nucleus relays motor impulses from basal ganglia to motor cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following thalamic nuclei projects to the cingulate gyrus?
questions.explanation: The anterior thalamic nucleus is part of the limbic system's Papez circuit. It receives input from the hippocampus via the mammillothalamic tract and projects to the cingulate gyrus, which is involved in emotion, memory, and pain perception. This circuit is essential for emotional processing and memory consolidation.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior thalamic nucleus projects to cingulate gyrus as part of Papez limbic circuit.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius connects:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius is a narrow channel passing through the midbrain that connects the third ventricle (anteriorly, at the level of the midbrain) with the fourth ventricle (posteriorly, at the pontomedullary junction). It is surrounded by the periaqueductal gray matter.
